egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg Omelet with Cheese, Meat and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled eggs with cheese, meat and tomatoes is a nutritious dish often served for breakfast or a light dinner. Eggs provide high‑quality protein, while cheese, meat and tomatoes add flavor, texture and additional nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most affordable sources of complete protein.
Cheese adds calcium and a creamy texture to the dish.
Meat (such as ham or bacon) contributes a rich taste and iron.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant with health‑supporting properties.
The omelet can be easily adapted to dietary preferences by using low‑fat cheese, lean meat or plant‑based protein alternatives.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat supply all essential amino acids, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese provides calcium important for bone and tooth health.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes contain lycopene and vitamin C, helping protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and meat are rich in B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat promotes lasting fullness.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Cheese and fatty meat can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or dairy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs or cheese.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cured meat and cheese can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beat the eggs with a splash of milk, pour into a hot pan, add chopped tomatoes, pre‑cooked meat and grated cheese. Cook to your preferred consistency and serve hot with whole‑grain toast or fresh vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently, adding a little milk or water to restore softness.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-ma.title: Egg Omelet or Scrambled Egg with Meat Made with Margarine

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet or scrambled eggs with meat cooked in margarine is a dish made from beaten eggs combined with pieces of meat (commonly ham or bacon) and a small amount of margarine. The dish was popular in the 1980s as a quick, hearty breakfast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: In 1987 margarine was cheaper and more widely used than butter in institutional cooking.
The combination of eggs and meat provides a complete set of essential amino acids.
The recipe can be adapted by swapping the meat for chicken, turkey, or plant‑based alternatives.
Traditionally the omelet was served with toast or bread, sometimes sprinkled with fresh herbs.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Eggs and meat are high‑quality protein sources needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Provides fats
items.content: Margarine adds energy and helps absorb fat‑soluble vitamins, but should be used in moderation.

items.title: High in saturated fats
items.content: Older margarine formulas may contain trans fats, which can increase cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Allergy to eggs or meat
items.content: Some people may experience allergic reactions to eggs or specific types of meat.

items.title: Sodium and preservatives in processed meat
items.content: Processed meats like ham or bacon often contain salt and nitrites, which should be considered in low‑sodium diets.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, add finely chopped meat, salt and pepper. Melt margarine in a skillet, pour in the egg mixture and cook over medium heat, stirring until the omelet is set but still tender. Serve hot with bread or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The cooked omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a skillet or microwave, adding a little margarine to prevent drying out.
